goals: Cut a dendrogram to get clusters
why: When you do not know the number of groups and want to see the structure at every level (product taxonomies, gene families, store hierarchies), a dendrogram tells the story.
explain: **Agglomerative** clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly **merges the two closest clusters** until one remains.
The merge history is drawn as a **dendrogram**, a family tree in which the height of each join shows how far apart the merged clusters were.

**Linkage** defines the distance between clusters: **Ward** (minimises within-cluster variance, the usual default), **complete** (farthest points), **average**, **single** (nearest points, which can produce long chains).
**Cut** the tree at a chosen height to get clusters. Large vertical gaps in the dendrogram suggest a natural number of groups.

example.title: Single linkage on five numbers
steps: Average daily orders (hundreds) for five outlets: A = 1, B = 2, C = 4, D = 10, E = 11
Merge {A, B} at height 1, then {D, E} at height 1 (the two smallest distances)
C to {A, B} = closest pair = min(3, 2) = 2; C to {D, E} = min(6, 7) = 6 → C joins {A, B} at height 2
{A, B, C} to {D, E} = closest pair C–D = 6 → final join at height 6
example.result: Merge heights 1, 1, 2, 6. The big jump from 2 to 6 says cut there: two groups, small outlets {A, B, C} and big outlets {D, E}.

mistakes: Running it on very large data: it needs pairwise distances (memory ~ n²).
Using single linkage on noisy data (chaining).
takeaways: Dendrogram shows structure at every level
Ward linkage is the usual default
use: Small to medium data (up to ~10k rows)
When a hierarchy or taxonomy is the goal

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster
Z = linkage([[1], [2], [4], [10], [11]], method="single")   # outlets A–E
print(Z[:, 2])                                           # merge heights [1. 1. 2. 6.]
print(fcluster(Z, t=2, criterion="maxclust"))            # {A, B, C} vs {D, E}
X = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(30, 2)); X[:15] += 4
print(fcluster(linkage(X, method="ward"), t=2, criterion="maxclust"))
# scipy.cluster.hierarchy.dendrogram(Z) draws the tree (needs matplotlib)

options: Each point as its own cluster

check.q: The height of a merge in a dendrogram shows…
options: The distance between the merged clusters

formula.tex: d_{\text{single}}(A,B) = \min_{a \in A,\, b \in B} d(a,b), \qquad d_{\text{complete}}(A,B) = \max_{a \in A,\, b \in B} d(a,b)
formula.plain: Single linkage: two groups are as close as their two closest members. Complete linkage: as far as their two farthest members.
